text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London ended lower after profit-taking pared gains from a fund-led rally earlier this week. October ended $1.50 easier at S328.29, after hitting a contract high of $330.20 on Tuesday. December ended down $1.30 at $322.50 per tonne.

Raw sugar futures in New York consolidated recent gains and ended lower, but the market held above key support targets, floor sources said. The benchmark October contract lost 10 points to end at 11.49 cents/lb, having ranged from 11.58 to 11.45 cents/lb. The rest of the board finished unchanged to 0.06 weaker.

Dealers expect prices to ease further and support is pegged at the previous contract high of 11.40 cents/lb. A push above resistance at Tuesday's high of 11.65 cents/lb in October would attract further fund buying and carry the market sharply higher. A lack of physical offtake and not very constructive fundamental news together with extremely high open interest levels make the market vulnerable to a sell-off.

EUROPE - Western Europe's sugar beet areas continued to be in a stable condition ended July 23. Barring unforeseen climatic events this development can be expected to continue over the next several weeks. In Italy recent rainfalls have improved growing conditions and in Spain crop conditions are stable as soil moisture is adequate.

In Eastern Europe heavy rainfall continued in Poland and the Czech beet areas during the week. Some improvement is expected over the coming week as drier weather occurs, but some losses have occurred due to flooding in the wetter areas. Moderate to heavy rainfall has also occurred from Hungary southward to Romania. The beet areas in the former Soviet Union reported near normal rainfall of 50-75 mm during the period under review. Soil moisture is somewhat in surplus but so far this has caused no problems. As long as drier weather moves into the region over the coming week, yield prospects should remain very good.

POLAND - A full assessment of the damages caused by the heavy flooding is still impossible. Communication with flooded areas is very difficult. According to industry sources only one sugar factory has so far been seriously damaged by water. The other factories are reported to be in good condition. It is hoped that the losses caused by the floods can be compensated by very good beet harvests in other parts of the country. The beet acreage in Poland is now pegged at 400,000 ha and sugar production 1997/98 could still reach 1.8 million tonnes, white value.

UKRAINE - The final area sown to beet in Ukraine is put at 1.076 million ha, sharply down from last year's 1.418 million. However, emergence and early growth is reported to be very good with 47 percent of the area in good condition, 43 percent in average condition and only 10 percent in below average condition. The final beet yield per ha is estimated to reach 20.2 tonnes and white sugar output is forecast at 2.7 million tonnes, unchanged from last year.

ITALY - Sugar imports in March 1997 amounted to 31,032 tonnes, raw value, down from 44,167 tonnes imported in 1996. This brought cumulative imports in the first eight months of 1996/97 (August/March) up to 257,710 tonnes compared to 238,545 tonnes in the like period the previous year. Total imports in 1995/96 reached 379,026 tonnes against 266,279 tonnes in 1994/95.
Major countries of origin in 1996/97 were Germany with 88,760 tonnes whites against 51,755 tonnes, France with 59,533 tonnes, down from 110,646 tonnes and Cuba with 17,291 tonnes raws against nil.

Sugar exports in March 1997 amounted to 7,437 tonnes which brought cumulative exports in August/March 1996/97 to 91,493 tonnes, down from 143,172 tonnes in 1995/96. Total exports in 1995/96 reached 170,210 tonnes compared to 124,787 tonnes in 1994/95. Major countries of destination in 1996/97 were Lebanon with 24,037 tonnes whites against 23,351 tonnes, Croatia with 18,555 tonnes compared to 12,304 tonnes and Greece with 17,405 tonnes, up from 28 tonnes.

The European Union awarded 52,600 tonnes of white sugar at a maximum refund of 39.600 Ecus per 100 kg at its weekly tender on July 23. Cumulative awards so far made under the 1996/97 series of tenders for the period up to July 23 reached 2,494,425 tonnes, which compares to 2,524,148 last year.
